KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

We will remain under the influence of cool high pressure at the 
surface through at least early on Friday. The airmass overhead is 
very dry as sampled by the 00z GYX upper air sounding. The sampled 
PWATs were at 0.31 inches which is close to the minimum for this 
time of year. Thus, with clear skies and light winds, conditions 
will be favorable for radiational cooling and frost formation in the 
sheltered valleys this morning. Winds will be a bit breezier on the 
hilltops and areas along and south of the coastal plain which may 
limit the frost potential here. Lows are forecast to mainly be in 
the 40s but some mid to upper 30s are likely in the northern valleys 
and portions of the interior. Frost Advisory remains in effect for 
portions of the Interior and Midcoast until 11z.

While the high brings cool and fair weather to northern New England, 
a developing storm system off the Carolina coast continues to 
organize to our south. The surf continues to build over the next few 
days as a long easterly fetch strengthens across the North Atlantic 
between the high overhead and the developing storm system. These 
waves bring increasingly large breaking surf and rip currents 
through the end of the week. 

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

It would not be a coastal party without some uncertainty bringing 
confidence down in the medium range. While all NWP systems agree on 
a strong early season coastal storm developing off the Mid Atlantic 
and drifting north before doing a loop, what they do not agree on is 
where that stall and capture takes place. For instance the 
deterministic GFS favors Cape Cod while the ECMWF tucks into NYC. 
Even their respective ensemble systems have little overlap between 
low locations. The ensembles are fairly agnostic on strength 
however, all featuring similar spread. So given how similar the 
different model suites with the upper air pattern, that leads to 
somewhat lower confidence on the outcomes locally. A farther 
northeast storm will bring greater impacts vs. one hanging off the 
Jersey Shore. Much like yesterday the impacts in order of confidence 
are as follows:

High surf...It will be several days of northeast winds along the 
longest possible fetch. Seas will build thru Sat before the 
weakening allows waves to diminish slowly thru the beginning of next 
week. Seas building to around 10 ft remains likely, but significant 
wave heights up to 15 ft are not out of the question if the 
closer/stronger tracks are realized. This will especially be true 
towards Jeffrey's Ledge where the fetch will be the longest.

Winds...This may be a 2/2A with coastal flooding below. A strong 
pressure gradient forecast to set up between the coastal storm and 
retreating high pressure. Both pressure systems are anomalous for 
this time of year. Northeast winds also tend to keep a fairly well 
mixed boundary layer thanks to cold advection. As a result those 
winds should be fairly consistently gusty beginning as early as Fri. 
It could be a greater than 48 hour period with wind gusts frequently 
in excess of 35 mph along the coast. The greatest area of concern 
will be Casco Bay south to the Seacoast. This is where strongest 
winds aloft are forecast as well as the greatest onshore component 
of those winds. The more extreme wind forecasts approaching 60 mph 
are becoming more unlikely. However a low end Wind Advisory remains 
possible, especially with leaves still on the trees for now. The 
window for the best possible mixing and gusts pushing 45 mph will be 
during the closest approach Sun. 

Coastal Flooding...With sustained northeast winds and building seas 
over several days we are primed to maximize the potential storm 
surge by the weekend. Thankfully astronomical tides are not peaking 
until next week, but they will be increasing thru the weekend. 
Because the astronomical tides are not super high there is lower 
confidence that we reach flood stage, but the combination of high 
water and pounding surf should lead to significant splashover at the 
very least. The Stevens Inst Flood Advisory System is below flood 
stage at Portland at this time Sat into Sun, but surge forecasts 
also remain less than 2 ft. Given the very favorable multi-cycle set 
up I tend to think we will come in closer to that number than 1 ft. 
This should be enough for water levels to get right up to flood 
stage.

Rainfall...This remains the lowest confidence impact of the bunch 
because it will be so dependent on storm track and there is such a 
wide range of possibilities at this point in time. The forecast 
stall and capture, with a looping surface low, is a favorable set up 
for fairly widespread soaking rains, even the farther southwest 
ECMWF cases. The late warm season moisture content and strong 
synoptic forcing does mean that some significant rainfall remains 
possible, and the ECMWF Ens especially continues to put a 20 to 30 
percent chance of 4 inches or more rainfall
